justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly constructive near-term view on the S&P 500, anchored around the 3,100–3,150 range. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 3,110 is driven primarily by short-term momentum and the assumption that no major overnight catalysts materially reprice risk. Markets tend to exhibit mean-reversion over very short windows when volatility is moderate, so I assumed the next session would be relatively contained around the prevailing level. At the one-week horizon, the slight drift upward to 3,125 reflects a mild positive bias from typical risk-asset behavior in the absence of shock events, combined with any residual momentum. At the one-month horizon, 3,150 incorporates a small equity risk premium return expectation, though this is tempered by the recognition that macro data releases, earnings, and policy signals over a month can shift sentiment meaningfully in either direction.

The confidence interval widths widen progressively across horizons, which reflects the standard statistical reality that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% interval of roughly 3,040 to 3,180 is fairly tight because intraday and overnight price moves, absent a major shock, tend to be bounded. At one week, the interval expands to 2,980–3,270, capturing the added variability from several trading sessions, potential economic data surprises, and geopolitical developments. By one month, the interval of 2,850–3,450 is quite wide and reflects genuine uncertainty around Federal Reserve communications, inflation prints, corporate earnings guidance, and broader global growth signals — any of which could shift the index by several percent independently.

There are specific tail risks that could push outcomes well outside my stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected hawkish Federal Reserve pivot, a significant credit event, escalating geopolitical conflict, or a sharp deterioration in labor market data could push the index below 2,850 within a month. A sudden liquidity crisis or systemic financial stress — the kind of event that is rare but not unprecedented — would be the clearest path to outcomes in the 2,600–2,700 range. On the upside, a surprise ceasefire in an active conflict zone, a dramatically dovish Fed pivot, or a strong earnings season beating elevated expectations could push the index above 3,450. These tail events are assigned low but non-trivial probability, and they are precisely why I kept the one-month interval as wide as I did.

Finally, I want to be transparent that these estimates carry meaningful model uncertainty on top of the market uncertainty already reflected in the intervals.
